passage.en: A stationery shop sells pens at ₹10, notebooks at ₹40 and files at ₹25 each. On Monday it sold 5 pens, 3 notebooks and 2 files; on Tuesday it sold 8 pens, 2 notebooks and 4 files. The owner writes the sales as a 2 × 3 matrix S (one row per day, columns pens, notebooks, files) and the prices as a 3 × 1 column matrix P, and computes SP.

stem.en: What is the order of the matrix SP?

explanation.en: S is 2 × 3 and P is 3 × 1. The inner orders match (3 = 3), and SP has order 2 × 1: one revenue figure for each day.

Assertion (A): For square matrices A and B of the same order, (A + B)² = A² + 2AB + B² always.
Reason (R): Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: (A + B)² = A² + AB + BA + B², which equals A² + 2AB + B² only when AB = BA. Because multiplication need not commute (R is true), A is false in general.

Assertion (A): For any square matrix A, the matrix A + Aᵀ is symmetric.
Reason (R): (A + Aᵀ)ᵀ = Aᵀ + (Aᵀ)ᵀ = Aᵀ + A.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: R shows that the transpose of A + Aᵀ is the matrix itself, which is the definition of a symmetric matrix. So both are true and R explains A.

stem.en: A and B are square matrices of the same order. Which statements are always true? (One or more options may be correct.)

options.en: If AB = A and BA = B, then A² = A

explanation.en: (A + B)² = A² + AB + BA + B², and AB ≠ BA in general (try A = [1 2; 0 1], B = [1 0; 3 1]). If AB = A and BA = B: A² = (AB)A = A(BA) = AB = A. (AB)′ = B′A′ is the reversal rule. (A + A′)′ = A′ + A, so A + A′ is symmetric.

stem.en: A = [1 1; 1 1]. Find the sum of all the entries of A⁵. (Give an integer.)

explanation.en: A² = 2A, so Aⁿ = 2ⁿ⁻¹A. Then A⁵ = 16A, whose four entries are all 16. Their sum is 64.

stem.en: The number of possible orders of a matrix having 18 elements is:

explanation.en: The order m × n must have mn = 18. The divisors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18, giving 6 orders: 1×18, 2×9, 3×6, 6×3, 9×2, 18×1.

stem.en: If X + Y = [5 2; 0 9] and X − Y = [3 6; 0 −1], then X equals:

explanation.en: Adding the two equations: 2X = [8 8; 0 8], so X = [4 4; 0 4] (and Y = [1 −2; 0 5]).

stem.en: Let N = [0 1; 0 0] and I the 2 × 2 identity. Which of the following are true? (One or more options may be correct.)

options.en: (I + N)ⁿ = I + nN for every natural number n

explanation.en: N² = O directly. Its determinant is 0, so N is not invertible. (I + N)(I − N) = I − N² = I. By the binomial theorem (I and N commute), (I + N)ⁿ = I + nN + (terms with N² = O).

stem.en: How many 3 × 3 skew-symmetric matrices have all their entries from {−1, 0, 1}? (Give an integer.)

explanation.en: A skew-symmetric matrix has zeros on the diagonal, and a₂₁, a₃₁, a₃₂ are fixed by a₁₂, a₁₃, a₂₃. Each of these three can be −1, 0 or 1: 3³ = 27.

stem.en: A = [3 1; −1 2] satisfies A² − 5A + 7I = O. Then A⁻¹ equals:

explanation.en: Multiply A² − 5A + 7I = O by A⁻¹: A − 5I + 7A⁻¹ = O, so A⁻¹ = (5I − A)/7.
